questions.stem: Which of the following statements are correct regarding mechanisms of depolarization, repolarization, hyperpolarization in a skeletal muscle action potential?Depolarization due to influx of Na + through voltage- gated channelsDepolarization due to influx of Na + through ligand – gated channelsRepolarization due to efflux of k + through voltage – gated channelRepolarization due to efflux of K + through ligand – gated channelHyperpolarization due to efflux of K+Select the correct answer from the given below code:
questions.solutionHtml:
1, 3 and 5 only
  • The depolarization, also called the rising phase, is caused when positively charged sodium ions (Na+) suddenly rush through open voltage-gated sodium channels into a neuron.
  • As additional sodium rushes in, the membrane potential actually reverses its polarity.
  • During this change of polarity the membrane actually develops a positive value for a moment (+40 millivolts).
  • The repolarization or falling phase is caused by the slow closing of sodium channels and the opening of voltage-gated potassium channels.
  • As a result, the membrane permeability to sodium declines to resting levels.
  • As the sodium ion entry declines, the slow voltage-gated potassium channels open and potassium ions rush out of the cell.
  • This expulsion acts to restore the localized negative membrane potential of the cell.
  • Hyperpolarization is a phase where some potassium channels remain open and sodium channels reset.
  • A period of increased potassium permeability results in excessive potassium efflux before the potassium channels close.
  • This results in hyperpolarization as seen in a slight dip following the spike



Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th Edition Page no. 97, 68.

questions.stem: True statements regarding skeletal muscle contraction are:Extracellular Ca++ not important for contractionCa++ released from mitochondriaCa++ releases from the sarcoplasmic reticulumVoltage – gated Ca++ channel on sarcolemma has no role in EC couplingCa++ channel on sarcoplasmic reticulum has no role in ECSelect the correct answer from the given below code:
questions.solutionHtml:
3 only
  • Only statement 3 is correct. During the contraction of the skeletal muscle, Ca is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
  1. Acetylcholine released from the axon terminal binds to receptors on the sarcolemma.
  2. An action potential is generated and travels down the T tubule.
  3. Ca2+ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in response to the change in voltage.
  4. Ca2+ binds troponin; Cross-bridges form between actin and myosin.
  5. Acetylcholinesterase removes acetylcholine from the synaptic cleft.
  6. Ca2+ is transported back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
  7. Tropomyosin binds active sites on actin causing the cross-bridge to detach.
  • Excitation contraction coupling refers to the process by which the membrane depolarization of the muscle fibre (excitation) leads to the contraction of the muscle.
  • The steps of excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal muscle are as follows:
  1. Motor-neuron discharge causes the release of acetylcholine at the motor endplate, which binds to the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
  2. This causes increased Na+ and K+ conductance in the endplate membrane leading to the generation of end-plate potential, which is a local potential.
  3. When the local endplate potential reaches a threshold for the muscle fibre an action potential is generated.
  4. The generated action potential passes inward through the T tubules leading to the spread of depolarisation.
  5. The depolarization of the muscle fibre causes the release of Ca from terminal cisterns of sarcoplasmic reticulum and diffusion to thick and thin filaments.
  6. The released calcium binds to troponin C uncovering myosin-binding sites on actin.
  7. The formation of cross-linkages between actin and myosin and sliding of thin on thick filaments causes contraction of the skeletal muscle.



Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th Edition Page no. 97, 68.

questions.stem: When a person changes posture from supine to standing :Increase in firing from baroreceptorDecrease in firing from baroreceptorVagal output to cardiac fibers increaseMesenteric VasoconstrictionIncreased cardiac contractilitySelect the correct answer from the given below code:
questions.solutionHtml:
2 and 5 only
  • When a person stands up from a lying down position, it causes pooling of the blood in the legs, due to gravity.
  • This reduces the venous return and causes a decrease in cardiac output.
  • Reduced cardiac output, leads to a fall in blood pressure, which in turn causes reduced firing from baroreceptors.
  • As a result, the vagal tone is suppressed leading to increased heart rate.


Ganong's Review Of Medical Physiology, 26th Edition Page no. 533, Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th Edition Page no. 222.

questions.stem: Macula densa formed by which part of nephron:
questions.solutionHtml:
DCT
  • The macula densa is formed by the DCT (Distal Convoluted Tubule) of the nephron.
  • The macula densa is a specialized region located at the junction between the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle and the early part of the DCT.



Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th Edition Page no. 209, 324, 339. Ganong's Review Of Medical Physiology, 26th Edition Page no - 693.

questions.stemHtml: This is a graph depicting the filterability of dextran through the kidney, 1 representing complete filtration and 0 representing no filtration. Choose substance A, B, C respectively:
questions.solutionHtml:
Polycationic, Neutral, Polyanionic
  • Let’s Understand This graphs phenomenon:-
  • Figure Above shows nfluence of the size and electrical charge of dextran on its filterability. A value of 1 indicates that it is filtered freely, whereas a value of zero indicates that it is not filtered. The filterability of dextrans between approximately 20 and 42 Å depends on charge.
  • Dextrans larger than 42 Å are not filtered regardless of charge, and polycationic dextrans and neutral dextrans smaller than 20 Å are freely filtered. The major proteins in plasma are albumin and immunoglobulins. Because the effective molecular radii of IgG (53 Å) and IgM (>100 Å) are greater than 42 Å, they are not filtered.
  • Although the effective molecular radius of albumin is 35 Å, it is a polyanionic protein, so it does not cross the filtration barrier to a significant degree.



Ganong's Review Of Medical Physiology, 26th Edition Page no. 667.

questions.stem: As filtrate flows through the renal tubules, which of the following is maximally reabsorbed:
questions.solutionHtml:
Glucose
  • Glucose is maximally reabsorbed in the renal tubules.
  • Glucose is actively reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubules (PCT) of the nephron. The glucose transporters in the PCT are highly efficient and can reabsorb almost all the filtered glucose, preventing its loss in the urine. This process is known as renal glucose reabsorption.


Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th Edition Page no. 349.

questions.stemHtml: Acid – base nomogram diagram is given below. Changes in PCO2 are by curve lines. Areas marked with A and D indicate which of the following conditions

options.label: C
options.text: Acute respiratory acidosis & Chronic respiratory alkalosis

questions.solutionHtml:
Chronic respiratory acidosis & metabolic acidosis

Let’s Focus on this graph :-

  • Notice that on the x-axis (pH), 7.4, normal pH is in the middle. Notice that it crosses the y-axis (bicarb), at 24. That location with coordinates of 7.4 on the x-axis and 24 on the y-axis is called normal.
  • Notice that the graph is like three intersecting curves drawn with a paintbrush with broad strokes. Notice that they are not straight lines but curves. The metabolic disorder curve runs from bottom-left to top right.
  • The chronic respiratory disorder curve runs from the top-left to the bottom-right. And the acute respiratory disorder curve runs from toward the middle from somewhat middle-left to somewhat bottom-right.



Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition Page 359.

questions.stem: Calculate respiratory quotient (RQ) in a patent with 50 kg body weight, CO2, Exhaled 200ml/min, and O2 consumed 250ml/min:
questions.solutionHtml:
0.8
  • The respiratory quotient is 0.8.
  • Respiratory Quotient is the ratio of carbon dioxide production to oxygen utilization.
  • In the given question, the CO2 production is 200 ml/min, while the O2 consumption is 250 ml/min.
  • Therefore, Respiratory quotient = 200/250 = 0.8
  • The respiratory quotient (RQ) is used for determining the metabolic utilization of various foods.
  • When carbohydrates are metabolized with one molecule of oxygen, one carbon dioxide molecule is released.
  • Therefore, the RQ of carbohydrates = 1.
  • When fats are oxidized, for every 100 molecules of oxygen consumed, 70 molecules of CO2 are released.
  • Thus, the RQ of fats is 0.70.
  • The respiratory quotient for proteins is 0.80.


Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th Edition Page no. 878.

questions.stem: In the diagram, a simple muscle twitch with a time trace below is recorded in a frog gastrocnemius muscle. Calculate the minimum tetanizing frequency of this muscle. Time tracer is done with a 100Hz tuning fork:
questions.solutionHtml:
17 per sec

Tetanizing frequency = 1/contraction period,

  • Where the contraction period is the time taken from latent period to maximum force of contraction.
  • In the given diagram, the time tracer was taken using a 100Hz tuning fork. Which means the tracer recorded 100 waves per second below the twitch graph.
  • Therefore, the duration of each wave in time tracer = 0.01 seconds.
  • Between the point B (end of latent period) to point C (maximum force of contraction), there are 6 waves.
  • Hence the duration of contraction = 6 x 0.01 = 0.06 seconds.
  • Thus, Tetanizing frequency = 100/6 = 16.66/sec= ~ 17/sec


Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th Edit Page no. 88, 89., Ganong's Review Of Medical Physiology, 26th Edition Page no. 105, 107.
